questions.stem: The Aborigines Advancement League was founded in Victoria in 1957. Its first field officer, who later became Governor of South Australia, was:
options: Eddie Koiki Mabo
Pastor Doug Nicholls
Charles Perkins
Vincent Lingiari
questions.explanation: Doug Nicholls, a Yorta Yorta man, worked for the League from its foundation and became Governor of South Australia in 1976. Charles Perkins led the 1965 Freedom Ride in New South Wales.

questions.stem: The 1965 Freedom Ride through western and northern New South Wales was led by:
options: Gary Foley and the activists who later set up the Aboriginal Tent Embassy in Canberra
Doug Nicholls and members of the Victorian Aborigines Advancement League
Charles Perkins and Student Action for Aborigines from the University of Sydney
Faith Bandler and the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders
questions.explanation: Perkins, an Arrernte and Kalkadoon man studying at the University of Sydney, led a busload of mostly non-Indigenous students to country towns in February 1965. Faith Bandler and FCAATSI led the 1967 referendum campaign.

questions.stem: The Freedom Ride drew on the American Civil Rights Movement mainly by:
options: organising a long boycott of country bus services like the Montgomery boycott
copying the US Freedom Riders' tactic of exposing segregation to the media
inviting Martin Luther King to lead the bus tour through country New South Wales
seeking a High Court ruling against segregation like Brown v Board of Education
questions.explanation: Like the 1961 US Freedom Rides, the students travelled by bus to confront segregation and made sure reporters and cameras followed. They used direct action and publicity, not court cases or boycotts.

questions.stem: At Moree in 1965 the Freedom Riders protested at the town swimming baths because:
options: the baths stood on land claimed by the local Aboriginal community
Aboriginal workers had built the pool but had never been paid for it
the state government planned to close the town's only public pool
a local council rule barred Aboriginal people from the pool
questions.explanation: Moree council had excluded Aboriginal people from the baths. The students escorted Aboriginal children into the pool amid a hostile crowd, and the confrontation made national news.

questions.stem: Which outcome best shows the historical significance of the Freedom Ride?
options: It led New South Wales to pass Australia's first state land rights Act in the following year
It ended segregation of pools, cinemas and hotels in every New South Wales town within weeks
It caused the federal government to abolish the New South Wales Aborigines Welfare Board
Press coverage showed city Australians racism in country towns, building support for change
questions.explanation: The Ride's main impact was on public opinion, helping create the climate for the 1967 referendum. Segregation ended unevenly, the Welfare Board was a state body abolished by New South Wales in 1969, and the state's land rights Act came only in 1983.

questions.stem: In the years before the 1967 referendum, FCAATSI and its supporters campaigned for a Yes vote mainly by:
options: occupying Parliament House until the government agreed to hold a vote
taking the Commonwealth to the High Court over section 127
calling a national strike of Aboriginal pastoral workers
collecting petitions and lobbying MPs to change the Constitution
questions.explanation: From the late 1950s campaigners led by figures such as Faith Bandler and Jessie Street gathered petitions with tens of thousands of signatures and lobbied members of parliament. When the vote came, it had support across parliament, so no official No case was put to voters.

questions.stem: On the same day in May 1967, voters also answered a question on the 'nexus' between the size of the House and the Senate. The contrast between the two results suggests that:
options: both questions passed, showing that referendums were easy to win at the time
the nexus question passed easily while the Aboriginal question barely passed
the Aboriginal question won unusual cross-party and popular support
voters were confused and voted Yes to both questions without reading them
questions.explanation: The nexus question was defeated, while the Aboriginal question passed with a huge majority in every state. Referendums rarely succeed in Australia, so the size of the Yes vote shows how far the civil rights campaign had moved opinion.

questions.stem: In August 1966 Vincent Lingiari led Gurindji stockmen and their families off Wave Hill station. The station was owned by:
options: the mining company Nabalco
the Commonwealth government
the Australian Agricultural Company
the British pastoral company Vestey's
questions.explanation: Wave Hill was run by the Vestey group, a British company. Nabalco was the mining company at Gove, challenged by the Yolngu in the Gove land rights case.

questions.stem: The Gurindji walk-off began as a protest over wages and conditions. It became central to the land rights movement because the Gurindji:
options: accepted a move to a government reserve close to Darwin
sought the return of their land at Wattie Creek (Daguragu)
won equal wages in court within weeks and went back to work
sued Vestey's in the High Court for the loss of their land
questions.explanation: The Gurindji set up camp at Wattie Creek and petitioned for their traditional land to be returned. Supported by unions, writers such as Frank Hardy and city activists, their strike lasted years and turned a wages dispute into a land claim.

questions.stem: In 1975 Prime Minister Whitlam poured soil into Vincent Lingiari's hand. The ceremony marked:
options: the passing of the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act
the end of all pastoral leases on Gurindji Country
the handing back of a lease over part of Gurindji Country
the recognition of native title across the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: Whitlam handed over a lease to part of the land, a powerful symbol of the return of land. The Northern Territory land rights Act passed under Fraser in 1976, and native title was not recognised until Mabo in 1992.

questions.stem: The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 was prepared under Whitlam but passed by the Fraser government. This is evidence that:
options: the Coalition had rejected the Woodward Royal Commission's recommendations
land rights in the Territory had support across the major parties
the Act was forced on the Fraser government by a ruling of the High Court
native title had already been recognised by the courts before 1976
questions.explanation: The Act grew out of the Woodward Royal Commission and was passed, in amended form, by a Coalition government. It created land councils and a claims process, but only for the Northern Territory. Courts did not recognise native title until 1992.

questions.stem: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy was set up outside Parliament House in Canberra on 26 January 1972, in response to:
options: the government's refusal to hold a referendum on a treaty with Aboriginal people
McMahon's statement rejecting land rights in favour of general purpose leases
the Senate's defeat of a bill that would have granted land rights across Australia
a Commonwealth decision to close all Aboriginal reserves in the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: On the eve of Australia Day 1972 McMahon announced that the government would offer leases for economic use, not land rights based on traditional ownership. Four young Aboriginal men set up a beach umbrella on the lawns, and the Embassy grew from there.

questions.stem: Why did the protesters call their camp an 'embassy'?
options: because the government had granted the camp a form of diplomatic status
to seek asylum for Aboriginal activists facing arrest in their home states
to show that Aboriginal people were treated as foreigners in their own land
because foreign embassies in Canberra had agreed to fund the protest camp
questions.explanation: The name made a political point about dispossession and sovereignty. The Embassy had no official status; police removed it in July 1972, and it was re-established several times.

questions.stem: The Black Power movement centred on Redfern in the early 1970s, with activists such as Gary Foley, emphasised:
options: assimilation into the wider community through education and work
leaving campaigns to be led by non-Indigenous allies and unions
full integration of Aboriginal services into state welfare boards
Aboriginal control of Aboriginal affairs and community services
questions.explanation: Black Power activists set up community-controlled bodies such as the Aboriginal Legal Service and Aboriginal Medical Service in Redfern. They rejected assimilation and paternalistic leadership, including from well-meaning non-Indigenous supporters.

questions.stem: How did decolonisation in Asia and Africa after 1945 influence Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander activists?
options: It persuaded most activists to give up land claims and support the assimilation policy
It led activists to campaign for Australia to withdraw from the United Nations
It convinced activists that change would come only through appeals to British courts
It offered examples of colonised peoples winning rights and self-determination
questions.explanation: As new nations won independence and the United Nations condemned racial discrimination, Australia's treatment of Aboriginal people drew international criticism. Activists used ideas of self-determination and human rights to frame their demands.

questions.stem: The claim that Aboriginal sovereignty was 'never ceded' differs from the main civil rights aims of the early 1960s because it:
options: questions colonisation itself instead of seeking equal treatment
seeks equal wages and access to public places such as pools, hotels and cinemas
accepts the doctrine of terra nullius but asks for compensation for lost land
focuses mainly on gaining the right to vote in state and federal elections
questions.explanation: Early civil rights campaigns sought equal treatment as citizens. The sovereignty argument, prominent from the Tent Embassy onward, holds that Aboriginal nations never gave up their sovereignty, so it questions the basis of Crown authority itself.

questions.stem: In 1988 Northern Territory leaders gave Prime Minister Hawke the Barunga Statement, calling for land rights, self-management and a treaty. Hawke responded by promising:
options: reserved seats for Aboriginal people in parliament
that a treaty would be concluded by 1990
an immediate national apology for past policies
a referendum to recognise Aboriginal sovereignty
questions.explanation: Hawke said there would be a treaty by 1990, but none was made. The government turned instead to a formal reconciliation process from 1991, which critics saw as a retreat from the treaty idea.

questions.stem: In 1979 the National Aboriginal Conference proposed a treaty it called a Makarrata. The Yolngu word refers to:
options: land returned to its owners after a court case
coming together to settle a dispute
the right to hunt and fish on one's own Country
a council of elders drawn from many nations
questions.explanation: Makarrata describes a process for resolving conflict and restoring relations. Supporters, including the non-Indigenous Aboriginal Treaty Committee led by H.C. Coombs, argued that a treaty was needed to settle the unfinished business of colonisation.

questions.stem: In the treaty debates of the 1980s, opponents such as John Howard argued that a treaty was wrong because:
options: a nation could not make a treaty with some of its own citizens
Aboriginal people had already been offered a treaty in 1967
the High Court had ruled that treaties were unconstitutional
only the Queen herself could sign a treaty in Australia
questions.explanation: Howard argued in 1988 that it was absurd for a nation to make a treaty with itself, a view that framed Aboriginal people only as citizens rather than as distinct peoples. Supporters replied that Aboriginal nations had never agreed to colonisation.

questions.stem: In Koowarta v Bjelke-Petersen (1982), a Wik man challenged Queensland's refusal to let an Aboriginal group buy a pastoral lease. The High Court held that:
options: the Racial Discrimination Act applied only in the federal territories
the Racial Discrimination Act was valid under the external affairs power
native title still existed over the pastoral lease and must be respected
Queensland's land laws overrode any Commonwealth law on discrimination
questions.explanation: The Court upheld the Act as implementing an international convention against racial discrimination. Queensland still blocked the purchase by turning the land into a national park, showing how state power could resist change.

questions.stem: In Mabo No 1 (1988) the High Court struck down a 1985 Queensland law that tried to extinguish any Meriam land rights retrospectively. It did so because the law:
options: had not been approved by Queensland voters at a referendum
breached a treaty Britain had signed with Torres Strait Islanders
had been passed without the assent of the Queensland Governor
was inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975
questions.explanation: Because the Queensland law removed rights only from Islanders, it conflicted with the Commonwealth's Racial Discrimination Act and was invalid under section 109. This cleared the way for the main case to be decided in 1992.

questions.stem: In Mabo v Queensland (No 2) in 1992 the High Court:
options: granted self-government to the Torres Strait Islands under Commonwealth law
rejected terra nullius and recognised the native title of the Meriam people
awarded compensation to all Torres Strait Islanders for the loss of their land
ruled that every pastoral lease in Australia had extinguished native title
questions.explanation: The Court held that the Meriam people of Mer held native title that had survived British annexation, rejecting the idea that the land had belonged to no one. Eddie Koiki Mabo had died months before the decision.

questions.stem: The Native Title Act 1993, passed by the Keating government, responded to the Mabo decision by:
options: extinguishing native title everywhere in return for a single payment
giving the state Supreme Courts sole power over all native title claims
setting up a process, with a tribunal, for deciding native title claims
returning all unallocated Crown land in Australia to its traditional owners
questions.explanation: The Act created the National Native Title Tribunal, validated past land grants and set rules for future dealings. Native title could be claimed only where it had not been extinguished, so most land was unaffected.

questions.stem: In the Wik decision of December 1996 the High Court found that:
options: pastoral leases on Cape York were invalid and the land must be returned
native title could coexist with pastoral leases, but the lease prevailed
pastoral leases had always extinguished any native title over the leased land
native title gave the Wik peoples exclusive possession of the leased land
questions.explanation: The Court held that a pastoral lease did not necessarily extinguish native title, but where the two conflicted, the lease prevailed. Pastoral and mining groups warned of uncertainty, and the government moved to amend the Native Title Act.

questions.stem: The Howard government's response to Wik, the 'Ten Point Plan', became the Native Title Amendment Act 1998. Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leaders argued that it:
options: repealed the Native Title Act and ended all future land claims
wound back native title rights in favour of pastoralists and miners
gave native title holders a veto over all new mining in Australia
created a treaty without first consulting the state governments
questions.explanation: The amendments limited the right to negotiate and confirmed extinguishment in many cases. Critics saw a retreat from the promise of Mabo, while supporters argued they gave certainty to landholders, showing how far land rights remained contested.

questions.stem: In 1969 Zelda D'Aprano chained herself to the doors of the Commonwealth Building in Melbourne to protest against:
options: unequal pay for women
conscription for Vietnam
the marriage bar for women
the lack of public child care
questions.explanation: D'Aprano was protesting during the 1969 Equal Pay Case. She and others later rode trams paying only part of the fare, to match the share of male wages women received.

questions.stem: The 1969 Equal Pay decision granted 'equal pay for equal work'. Why did it benefit relatively few women at first?
options: It covered only women who were the main earners for their families
Most women did female-dominated jobs with no male equivalent
It applied only to women employed in the Commonwealth public service
The High Court overturned it in 1970 after an appeal by employers
questions.explanation: Because most women did 'women's work', they could not show they did the same work as men. The 1972 decision of 'equal pay for work of equal value' widened the principle, and in 1974 the adult minimum wage was extended to women.

questions.stem: The Women's Electoral Lobby, formed in 1972, tried to influence government mainly by:
options: organising a national general strike of women workers in 1972
campaigning for women to gain the vote in federal elections
surveying candidates on women's issues and publishing their answers
standing its own candidates for every seat in the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: WEL rated candidates at the 1972 election on issues such as equal pay, child care and abortion, and then lobbied governments. Women had held the federal vote since 1902.

questions.stem: In 'Damned Whores and God's Police' (1975), Anne Summers argued that Australian women had been:
options: given equality with men in work and politics from the time of Federation
mostly respectable settlers whose convict history had been invented
uninterested in the vote until the women's liberation movement began
confined to two stereotypes, as either 'damned whores' or 'God's police'
questions.explanation: Summers argued that since colonial times women had been cast either as immoral or as the moral guardians of society, both roles serving men's interests. Her book was influential in the women's liberation movement.

questions.stem: The 1969 Menhennitt ruling in Victoria (R v Davidson) was significant for reproductive rights because it:
options: made the oral contraceptive pill available in Australia for the first time
removed abortion from Victoria's Crimes Act and treated it as health care
held abortion lawful if needed to protect a woman's life or health
legalised abortion on request throughout Australia under Commonwealth law
questions.explanation: Justice Menhennitt ruled that an abortion was not unlawful if a doctor reasonably believed it necessary to protect a woman from serious danger to her life or physical or mental health. Abortion stayed in the Crimes Act; Victoria decriminalised it only in 2008, and the pill had been available since 1961.

questions.stem: The Family Law Act 1975 changed divorce in Australia by:
options: making 12 months' separation the only ground, so fault no longer had to be proved
allowing divorce only where adultery, cruelty or desertion could be proved in court
giving fathers automatic custody of children after a marriage ended
requiring couples to obtain a church annulment before a civil divorce
questions.explanation: The Act introduced no-fault divorce and set up the Family Court. Under the old law a spouse had to prove grounds such as adultery or cruelty, which the new Act replaced.

questions.stem: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 rested on the Commonwealth's external affairs power because it gave effect to:
options: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948
the race power as amended by the 1967 referendum
the conciliation and arbitration power in section 51(xxxv)
the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
questions.explanation: Because Australia had ratified the convention, the Commonwealth could legislate against sex discrimination in areas such as employment and education. The Universal Declaration is not a binding treaty, so it could not support the Act in the same way.

questions.stem: On 11 November 1975 Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed the Whitlam government after:
options: the Senate blocked supply and Whitlam refused to call an election
the House of Representatives passed a motion of no confidence in Whitlam
the High Court ruled that the government's overseas loans were unlawful
Whitlam lost a double dissolution election to the Coalition
questions.explanation: The Coalition-controlled Senate deferred the budget bills, and Whitlam would not advise an election. Kerr used the reserve powers to withdraw his commission while Labor still held a majority in the House.

questions.stem: After dismissing Whitlam, Kerr commissioned Malcolm Fraser as caretaker Prime Minister on condition that he:
options: held a referendum on the Governor-General's reserve powers
governed until the next scheduled election in 1977
secured supply and advised an immediate double dissolution
formed a national unity government with Labor ministers
questions.explanation: The Senate passed supply that afternoon, and parliament was dissolved for an election on 13 December 1975, which the Coalition won heavily.

questions.stem: Which argument did critics of the Dismissal most often make?
options: The High Court had declared the dismissal unlawful shortly after the election
Blocking supply broke convention, and Whitlam still held the House
The Governor-General had no constitutional power to appoint any Prime Minister
The Queen had personally ordered Kerr to dismiss Whitlam on the advice of Fraser
questions.explanation: Critics argued that the Senate should not block supply and that Kerr acted without warning Whitlam, against a government with a House majority. Supporters replied that the Constitution gave the Senate power over money bills and the Governor-General reserve powers.

questions.stem: In 1975 two state parliaments filled Labor Senate vacancies with people not chosen by Labor, helping the Coalition control the Senate. The lasting result was:
options: the removal of the Senate's power to block or defer supply bills
a 1977 law letting the Senate dismiss a Governor-General
a ban on state premiers taking part in Senate appointments
a 1977 referendum requiring casual vacancies to go to the same party
questions.explanation: The 1977 casual vacancies referendum passed, writing the convention into section 15. The Senate's power over supply was not changed, so the debate over 1975 continues.

questions.stem: The Prices and Incomes Accord of 1983 was an agreement between:
options: the Coalition parties and the ACTU
the Reserve Bank and the Treasury
the Labor Party and the ACTU
the Labor Party and employer groups
questions.explanation: Negotiated before the 1983 election, the Accord bound the incoming Hawke Labor government and the Australian Council of Trade Unions to cooperate on wages and economic policy.

questions.stem: Under the Accord, unions accepted wage restraint in return for:
options: a constitutional guarantee of workers' right to strike
the abolition of the Arbitration Commission's powers
a promise to nationalise the major private banks
a 'social wage' including Medicare and wider superannuation
questions.explanation: The government offered improvements to the social wage, such as Medicare from 1984 and award superannuation, while unions kept wage claims in check to fight inflation and unemployment.

questions.stem: The first Sydney Mardi Gras, on 24 June 1978, was:
options: a night street march for gay rights that ended in police arrests
a celebration of the decriminalisation of homosexuality in New South Wales
a government-sponsored tourism parade along Oxford Street
a march to Parliament House after a High Court ruling on equality
questions.explanation: The march was part of an international day of gay solidarity marking the Stonewall riots. Police broke it up and arrested dozens of people. New South Wales did not decriminalise male homosexuality until 1984.

questions.stem: After the first Mardi Gras, many of those arrested lost their jobs or were outed to their families because:
options: the law required employers to dismiss anyone who was arrested
a newspaper published their names, addresses and occupations
the police broadcast their photographs on the evening news
they were all sentenced to long prison terms for the march
questions.explanation: The Sydney Morning Herald printed details of those arrested, with serious consequences for many of them. The newspaper apologised in 2016. The episode shows how far social attitudes and the law punished people for their sexuality.

questions.stem: Which state was the first to decriminalise male homosexual acts, in 1975?
options: New South Wales
Tasmania
South Australia
Victoria
questions.explanation: South Australia under the Dunstan government led the way. Victoria followed in 1980, New South Wales in 1984 and Tasmania last, in 1997.

questions.stem: Tasmania was the last state to decriminalise homosexuality, in 1997. Which development put the most pressure on it to change?
options: A 1994 UN finding that its laws breached the right to privacy
A 1991 High Court ruling that struck down Tasmania's laws as unconstitutional
A 1994 national referendum that approved equal rights for gay and lesbian people
A direction from the Governor-General to the Tasmanian Governor in 1996
questions.explanation: In Toonen v Australia the UN Committee found Tasmania's laws breached the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Commonwealth then passed a privacy law to override them, and Tasmania repealed them in 1997 as a High Court challenge was under way.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates continuity and change in Aboriginal land rights between 1788 and 1998?
options: Courts consistently recognised Aboriginal title from Batman's treaty onwards
Terra nullius fell in 1992, but the 1998 amendments showed land rights remained contested
Land rights were secured by the 1967 referendum and were not seriously challenged again
Native title was recognised in the colonial constitutions of the 1850s and grew steadily
questions.explanation: For most of the period the law treated the land as available for the Crown to grant. Mabo marked a profound change, but Wik and the 1998 amendments show that resistance to land rights continued.

questions.stem: Comparing South Australia's 1894 suffrage law with women's liberation in the 1970s, which judgement about change is best supported?
options: Political rights came early, but equality in pay, work and family life took much longer
Women won full economic equality in 1894, so the later movement focused only on sexuality
Women gained no political rights at all until the women's liberation movement of the 1970s
The 1970s movement reversed the gains of 1894 by rejecting parliamentary politics
questions.explanation: Australian women won the vote and the right to stand early by world standards, but equal pay, equal opportunity laws and reproductive rights were still being fought for in the 1970s and 1980s, showing deep continuities in gender inequality.
